unit-alg-0101.title: Topic 1 · 1-1 Key Features of Functions
unit-alg-0101.srcName: enVision Algebra 2, Lesson 1-1 Key Features of Functions (Drive)

summary.text: Lesson 1-1 from the enVision Algebra 2 student edition: reading the key features of linear, quadratic and absolute value functions off an equation or a graph — domain and range in both set-builder and interval notation, x- and y-intercepts, zeros, the intervals where a function is positive or negative, where it increases or decreases, maximums and minimums, and average rate of change over an interval.

why.text: Everything after this lesson assumes you can describe a graph precisely and quickly. Topic 1 keeps reusing this vocabulary, and Test 1 will expect the notation to be exact — a round bracket where a square one belongs is a wrong answer even when you understood the graph perfectly.

objectives.text: Write a domain and range in both set-builder and interval notation
Find x- and y-intercepts from an equation, and connect the x-intercepts to the zeros
Identify the intervals where a function is positive, negative, increasing or decreasing
Calculate and interpret an average rate of change over an interval
Keep "positive" and "increasing" apart, since the book flags that confusion explicitly

parentNote.text: Built from the 1-1 student edition. Two things to watch. First, the notation is where marks get lost: parenthesis versus square bracket, and infinity always taking a parenthesis. Several questions test only that. Second, the lesson's own listed common error — confusing a positive function value with a positive rate of change — has a card and two questions of its own, because a graph can be below the axis and climbing at the same time and that genuinely trips people. Every scenario here is fresh rather than lifted from her exercises; the book's problems stay her homework. All arithmetic re-derived independently.

nextUp.text: Cards first — this lesson is mostly vocabulary, and the quiz assumes you have the words. Then quiz rounds.

cards.def:
**The set of every input a function is allowed to take.**
• On a graph, read it left to right along the x-axis.
• A real-world domain is usually narrower than the algebra allows — time cannot be negative.

**The set of every output a function actually produces.**
• On a graph, read it bottom to top along the y-axis.
• Ask what the function CAN reach, not what it happens to hit at the points you plotted.

**A description of a set: a variable, a bar, then the rule the variable obeys.**
• {y | y is an integer and y ≥ 10} reads "all y such that y is an integer at least 10".
• The bar means "such that".

**A continuous set written as its two endpoints, low to high.**
• (−5, 0] is every number greater than −5 and up to and including 0.
• Always low endpoint first, then high.
cards.hint: Two numbers and two brackets carry everything set-builder needs a sentence for.

cards.def:
**Square bracket means the endpoint is included; parenthesis means it is not.**
• [−3, ∞) includes −3 itself.
• (−∞, 7) stops just short of 7 and never reaches it.
• Infinity always takes a parenthesis — you can never arrive at it.
cards.hint: Square corner = the door is open, come in. Round = stop at the doorway.

cards.def:
**An input that makes the output 0.**
• Same numbers as the x-intercepts — a zero is where the graph crosses the x-axis.
• Find them by setting the whole function equal to 0 and solving.
cards.hint: Zero of the FUNCTION means the output is zero, not the input.

cards.def:
**The x-coordinate where the graph crosses the x-axis.**
• Find it by setting y = 0 and solving for x.
• A graph can have several, or none at all.

**The y-coordinate where the graph crosses the y-axis.**
• Find it by substituting x = 0.
• A function has at most one — two would mean one input with two outputs.
cards.hint: One input, one output. That is why there is never more than one y-intercept.

cards.def:
**The x-intervals where the graph sits ABOVE the x-axis.**
• Positive means the output is greater than 0, so you read it off the y-values.
• At an x-intercept the function is neither positive nor negative, so those points are excluded — the intervals use parentheses.

**The x-intervals where the graph sits BELOW the x-axis.**
• Answer with x-intervals even though the test is about y-values. That swap is the usual slip.

**Increasing means the graph rises as you read left to right; decreasing means it falls.**
• Always judged left to right, as x grows.
• Reported as x-intervals, never y-intervals.
cards.hint: Trace it like a sentence: left to right. Uphill is increasing.

cards.def:
**Positive is about WHERE the graph is; increasing is about WHICH WAY it is going.**
• A function can be negative and increasing at once — climbing, but still below the axis.
• The book flags this as the common error, and it is.
cards.hint: Below the axis and climbing: negative, increasing. Both true, no contradiction.

cards.def:
**The maximum is the greatest output a function reaches; the minimum is the least.**
• A relative maximum is the highest point over some interval, not necessarily the whole graph.

**The change in output divided by the change in input, over an interval [a, b].**
• It is exactly the slope of the straight line joining the two endpoints.
• It says nothing about what happened in between — a rate of 0 does not mean nothing moved.
cards.hint: It is a slope. If you can find slope between two points, you can already do this.

cards.def:
**Linear y = x, constant y = 1, quadratic y = x², absolute value y = |x|.**
• All four have domain (−∞, ∞).
• y = x² and y = |x| both have range [0, ∞), both decrease on (−∞, 0) and increase on (0, ∞).
• y = 1 has range {y | y = 1} and no x-intercept at all.

**Find the vertex first — for a parabola opening upward it is the minimum, and the range starts there.**
• y = x² − 3 has its vertex at (0, −3), so the range is [−3, ∞).
• Square bracket, because the vertex value is actually reached.

questions.q: What does the domain of a function describe?
opts: Every input the function is allowed to take
Where the graph crosses the x-axis
The interval where the graph is rising
questions.hint: Inputs go in, outputs come out. Which one is the domain?
steps: A function takes an input and returns an output.
The domain is the collection of allowed inputs.
The outputs form the range. So the domain is every input the function can take.

ex.main: **Every input the function is allowed to take.** Read it along the x-axis, left to right.
ex.tip: Domain and x both come earlier in the alphabet. Range and y come later.

questions.q: In interval notation, what does a square bracket mean?
opts: The endpoint is included in the set
questions.hint: One bracket says "come in", the other says "stop just short".
steps: Interval notation marks each endpoint as included or excluded.
A parenthesis excludes the endpoint.
A square bracket includes it. So [−3, ∞) contains −3 itself.

ex.main: **The endpoint is included.** Which is why infinity never gets one — you cannot include a number you never reach.
ex.tip: Read [−3, ∞) aloud as "from −3, and −3 counts, upward forever".

questions.q: What is a zero of a function?
opts: An input that makes the output 0
An output of 0 for every input
The value of the function at x = 0
questions.hint: The name describes what the OUTPUT does, not the input.
steps: A zero is a value of x you feed in.
Feeding it in makes the function return 0.
That is the same as the graph touching the x-axis, so the zeros are the x-intercepts.

ex.main: **An input that makes the output 0.** Zeros and x-intercepts are the same numbers under two names.
ex.tip: The value at x = 0 is the y-intercept — the opposite question.

questions.q: The graph of a function lies below the x-axis for every x between −2 and 5. On that interval, the function is:
questions.hint: Below the axis means the y-values are what?
steps: Below the x-axis means every output there is less than 0.
An output less than 0 is a negative value.
So the function is negative on (−2, 5). Whether it rises or falls there is a separate question.

ex.main: **Negative.** Positive and negative describe where the graph SITS. Increasing and decreasing describe which way it MOVES.
ex.tip: A graph can be negative and increasing at the same time — below the axis, climbing.

questions.q: What is the y-intercept of a function found by doing?
questions.hint: The y-axis is the vertical line where x is zero.
steps: Every point on the y-axis has x-coordinate 0.
So the graph meets the y-axis when x = 0.
Substitute x = 0 and the value you get out is the y-intercept.

ex.main: **Substituting x = 0.** Setting y = 0 instead gives you the x-intercepts, which is the other half of the pair.
ex.tip: x-intercept: set y = 0. y-intercept: set x = 0. They cross over, and that is the trap.

questions.q: The average rate of change of f over [a, b] is the same as which of these?
opts: The slope of the line joining (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b))
The maximum value of f on [a, b]
The length of the interval, b − a
questions.hint: Change in output over change in input — where have you seen that fraction before?
steps: Average rate of change is (f(b) − f(a)) divided by (b − a).
The numerator is a change in y and the denominator is a change in x.
Rise over run is slope. So it is the slope of the segment joining the two endpoints.

ex.main: **The slope of the line joining the two endpoints.** Nothing new to memorise here — it is slope with a longer name.
ex.tip: Draw the straight line between the endpoints. Its steepness IS the answer.

questions.q: Write the set {x | x is a real number} in interval notation.
questions.hint: All real numbers stretch forever in both directions. And what bracket does infinity always take?
steps: Every real number is allowed, so the set runs from negative infinity to positive infinity.
Infinity is never included, because it is not a number you can reach.
So both ends take parentheses: (−∞, ∞).

ex.main: **(−∞, ∞).** Square brackets on infinity is the single most common notation slip in this lesson.
ex.tip: Infinity always gets a round bracket. No exceptions.

questions.q: What is the range of y = x² + 4?
questions.hint: Find the lowest point first. Can x² ever be negative?
steps: x² is never negative — the smallest it can be is 0, at x = 0.
So the smallest value of x² + 4 is 0 + 4 = 4.
The function reaches 4 exactly, and grows without bound above it.
So the range is [4, ∞), with a square bracket because 4 is actually attained.

ex.main: **[4, ∞).** The vertex sits at (0, 4), and for an upward parabola the vertex value is the minimum.
ex.tip: For any y = x² + k, the range is [k, ∞). Find the vertex and you have the answer.

questions.q: A water tank holds 600 L and drains at 15 L per minute until empty. What is the domain of the function giving the volume left after x minutes?
questions.hint: The domain is time here. When does the story start, and when does it stop making sense?
steps: x is time in minutes, and time cannot be negative, so x ≥ 0.
The tank empties when 15x reaches 600, that is x = 600 ÷ 15 = 40 minutes.
After 40 minutes the story is over — there is nothing left to drain.
So the domain is [0, 40], both endpoints included.

ex.main: **[0, 40].** The algebra would happily accept any x; the situation is what closes the interval at both ends.
ex.tip: The range here would be [0, 600] — the volumes, not the times. Do not mix the two up.

questions.q: What are the x-intercepts of y = |x| − 5?
questions.hint: Set the output to 0 and remember that absolute value has two ways to get there.
steps: Add 5 to both sides: |x| = 5.
Absolute value 5 means x is 5 units from zero, in either direction.
So x = 5 or x = −5. Both are x-intercepts.

ex.main: **−5 and 5.** Forgetting the negative solution is the standard mistake with absolute value.
ex.tip: |x| = c always gives two answers when c is positive, one when c is 0, and none when c is negative.

questions.q: For what interval is f(x) = x² − 16 negative?
questions.hint: Find the zeros first, then ask whether the parabola dips below the axis between them or outside them.
steps: Find the zeros: x² − 16 = 0 gives x² = 16, so x = −4 and x = 4.
The parabola opens upward, so it dips below the x-axis BETWEEN its two zeros.
Test a point inside, say x = 0: 0 − 16 = −16, which is negative. Confirmed.
So the function is negative on (−4, 4), with parentheses because it is zero, not negative, at the endpoints.

ex.main: **(−4, 4).** Outside that interval it is positive. Testing one point in the middle is the fastest way to be sure.
ex.tip: Endpoints are always excluded here: at a zero the function is neither positive nor negative.

questions.q: For what values of x is g(x) = 5 − |x| increasing?
questions.hint: The minus sign in front of the absolute value flips the usual V. Sketch it before you answer.
steps: g(x) = 5 − |x| is an upside-down V with its peak at (0, 5).
Reading left to right, the graph climbs up to the peak.
It reaches the peak at x = 0 and falls after that.
So it is increasing on (−∞, 0) and decreasing on (0, ∞).

ex.main: **(−∞, 0).** The peak is a maximum, so the graph rises before it and falls after — the reverse of a plain V.
ex.tip: Sketch the vertex first. Everything about increasing and decreasing follows from which way it opens.

questions.q: A phone plan costs $30 for the first 5 GB and then $10 per extra GB. What is the average rate of change of cost over the interval [0, 5] GB?
questions.hint: Work out the cost at each end of the interval first, then subtract.
steps: At 0 GB the cost is $30 — the plan charges that up front.
At 5 GB the cost is still $30, because the first 5 GB are included.
Change in cost is 30 − 30 = 0; change in data is 5 − 0 = 5.
Average rate of change is 0 ÷ 5 = 0 dollars per GB.

ex.main: **0 dollars per GB.** A rate of change of zero means the output did not move across that interval — the cost is flat there.
ex.tip: A zero rate of change is real information: it says "nothing changed", not "nothing happened".

questions.q: What is the average rate of change of f(x) = x² over the interval [1, 4]?
questions.hint: Compute f at both endpoints, then divide the difference by the width of the interval.
steps: Change in output: 16 − 1 = 15. Change in input: 4 − 1 = 3.
Average rate of change = 15 ÷ 3 = 5.

ex.main: **5.** Note it is not the slope at any single point — it is the slope of the line joining (1, 1) to (4, 16).
ex.tip: A curve has a different steepness everywhere. Average rate of change smooths that into one number.

questions.q: A student says the function graphed below the x-axis on (−3, 1) and rising throughout that interval is "both negative and increasing, which is impossible". What is wrong with that claim?
opts: Nothing is impossible — negative describes position, increasing describes direction
A negative function can never increase
The student mixed up domain and range
The intervals should have been written with square brackets
questions.hint: Ask what each word is actually measuring.
steps: "Negative" is a claim about the y-values: they are below zero.
"Increasing" is a claim about direction: as x grows, y grows.
A graph can sit below the axis and still climb toward it — think of −8, then −5, then −2.
Both statements are true at once, so there is no contradiction.

ex.main: **Nothing is impossible.** Negative is about WHERE, increasing is about WHICH WAY. The book flags exactly this as the common error.
ex.tip: A value can rise for a long time before it turns positive. A bank balance climbing out of overdraft is the same idea.

questions.q: The average rate of change of a hiker's elevation over [0, 3] hours is 0 ft/h. Which conclusion is justified?
opts: They finished at the same elevation they started, whatever happened in between
They did not move at all during the three hours
They walked on flat ground the entire time
They descended for the whole three hours
questions.hint: The formula only looks at two points. What can it possibly know about the middle?
steps: Average rate of change uses only the endpoint values: (f(3) − f(0)) ÷ 3.
For the result to be 0, the numerator must be 0, so f(3) = f(0).
That means the start and end elevations match.
The formula never inspects the middle, so a climb followed by an equal descent gives exactly the same answer as standing still.

ex.main: **They finished at the same elevation they started.** Everything else claims to know about the interior, which this measurement cannot see.
ex.tip: Whenever a rate of change is 0, ask "same endpoints, or genuinely nothing happening?" The formula cannot tell you.

questions.q: Which key features would let you tell the graph of y = x² apart from the graph of y = |x| if you could not see them?
opts: Neither domain, range, nor intervals of increase — those are identical for both
The intervals where each is increasing, which differ
questions.hint: Check the concept summary column by column before picking.
steps: Both have domain (−∞, ∞).
Both have range [0, ∞).
Both decrease on (−∞, 0) and increase on (0, ∞), and both have their only intercept at the origin.
So every key feature in the summary matches — the shape between the points is what differs, and no single key feature captures it.

ex.main: **None of those features separate them.** Key features are a summary, not a fingerprint. Two genuinely different functions can share all of them.
ex.tip: This is why you sketch. A list of features narrows the possibilities; it rarely pins down one curve.

questions.q: A function has domain [0, 12], is increasing on (0, 5), decreasing on (5, 12), and has a maximum of 40. What must be true?
questions.hint: Where does a graph that climbs and then falls reach its highest point?
steps: The function rises up to x = 5 and falls after it.
So the highest value it ever reaches is at the turning point, x = 5.
The maximum is given as 40, so f(5) = 40.
The range cannot be pinned down: nothing here says the lowest value is 0.

ex.main: **f(5) = 40.** The turn from increasing to decreasing is where the maximum lives — that is what a maximum means.
ex.tip: You cannot name the range without knowing the endpoint values. Not every question has enough information.

questions.q: Why are the endpoints excluded when you report the intervals where a function is positive?
opts: At an x-intercept the function equals 0, which is neither positive nor negative
Because interval notation always uses parentheses
Because the function is undefined there
Because the endpoints belong to the range instead
questions.hint: What is the actual output value at an x-intercept?
steps: The endpoints of a positive interval are the x-intercepts.
At an x-intercept the output is exactly 0.
Zero is not greater than 0, so the function is not positive there. It is not less than 0 either, so it is not negative.
Since it is neither, those points are left out of both intervals — hence parentheses.

ex.main: **At an x-intercept the function equals 0, which is neither positive nor negative.** The exclusion is a fact about the value, not a notation habit.
ex.tip: Interval notation uses square brackets freely elsewhere — for domain and range especially. Here the maths forbids them.

questions.q: The graph of y = −0.5x + 6 is positive on (−∞, 12) and negative on (12, ∞). What happens at x = 12?
opts: The function equals 0 — it is the x-intercept, and it is neither positive nor negative
The graph changes from increasing to decreasing
questions.hint: Substitute 12 and see what comes out.
steps: So the graph passes through (12, 0), which is the x-intercept.
At that single point the output is 0, so it is neither positive nor negative.
The line keeps decreasing straight through it — the boundary is about sign, not direction.

ex.main: **It equals 0 — the x-intercept.** A linear function never changes between increasing and decreasing; its slope is the same everywhere.
ex.tip: The sign of a function and the direction of a function change at different places, for different reasons.
